sentences.text: Iguanodon was a large, bulky plant-eater that could grow to lengths of 9 to 11 meters and weigh as much as 4.5 metric tons.
These animals were capable of moving on two legs or four legs depending on the situation.
The lower jaw of this dinosaur featured a toothless, scoop-shaped front that looks similar to the structure found in two-toed sloths and the extinct ground sloth Mylodon.
This genus is one of the three original groups used to define the entire Dinosauria clade, alongside Megalosaurus and Hylaeosaurus.
A banquet for twenty guests was once held inside the famous standing sculpture of this dinosaur before the artwork was finished.
When walking on two legs, the animal could reach a top speed of 24 km/h, but it was unable to gallop while on four legs.
Scientists processed bones from a specimen in 2003 and successfully found identifiable proteins like phosphoproteins and proteoglycans within a rib.
The genus name was established in 1825 by the English geologist Gideon Mantell after examining fossils discovered in England.
While a popular story says Mary Ann Mantell found the first teeth in Tilgate Forest in 1822, evidence indicates Gideon Mantell actually discovered them himself.
By 1849, Mantell realized the animal had slender front limbs rather than the heavy, elephant-like build previously assumed.
A specific specimen from Maidstone, known as the Mantel-piece and cataloged as NHMUK 3741, was later removed from the genus.
With a straight tail and back, the dinosaur likely kept its body horizontal to the ground, using its arms for support when needed.
The species I. bernissartensis is famous for many skeletons found in the Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation at Bernissart, with extra remains discovered across Europe.
The massive size of the largest species allowed it to reach food growing 4 to 5 meters high in trees.
David Norman proposed that their diet consisted of horsetails, cycads, and conifers.
However, iguanodontians in general are thought to have evolved alongside the rise of flowering plants during the Cretaceous.
Fossils from Nehden show a wide range of ages, suggesting I. bernissartensis may have lived in groups.
New analyses indicate at least three high-mortality events happened over a brief period of 10 to 100 years, though this does not prove herd living.
Research published in 2026 interprets I. bernissartensis as likely being an obligate quadruped.
A 2026 study provided new information regarding the variability of skull shapes in Iguanodon.
One fossil specimen shows evidence of a fractured hip bone and an injury to the ischium.
Two other individuals exhibited osteoarthritis, indicated by bone overgrowths known as osteophytes in their anklebones.
Iguanodon belongs to the larger group Iguanodontia, which also includes duck-billed hadrosaurs.
This genus gives its name to the clade Iguanodontia, a populous group of ornithopods known from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous.
Iguanodon lived during the early Lower Cretaceous period, between 126 and 120 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
The genus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 154.8 and 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Dollo's reconstruction of Iguanodon was accurate, as the tail was likely straight rather than bent, supported by evidence of ossified tendons.
The exact function of Iguanodon thumb spikes is debated, with hypotheses suggesting they were used for defense or foraging.
In 2026, Rotatori and colleagues suggested that Delapparentia is a distinct taxon related to Magnamanus and I. galvensis, proposing a new genus name for the latter.
